description: 按 Career OS JD 缺口补充的公开技术测评原题；题干、选项和解释均直接来自 Open Quiz Commons，不新增原创题。覆盖测试质量、系统运维与自动化。

source.selection_basis: Career OS jobs 表的 software-testing-ops、technical-support-fae、ai-rag 题型缺口映射

questions.title: What is the primary advantage of `pytest` assertions over the standard `unittest` library?
options: A. You must use specific methods like `assertIsInstance`
B. You can use the plain Python `assert` keyword
C. It requires a special DSL (Domain Specific Language)
D. Assertions are disabled by default for speed
questions.explanation: Pytest uses 'assertion rewriting' to provide detailed failure messages while allowing developers to use the simple, native Python `assert` keyword.
questions.source_text: What is the primary advantage of `pytest` assertions over the standard `unittest` library?

questions.title: What is a 'fixture' in `pytest`?
options: A. A permanent bug in the code
B. A function that provides a baseline/setup for tests to run reliably
C. A plugin used to export results to HTML
D. A test that is guaranteed to pass
questions.explanation: Fixtures are functions decorated with `@pytest.fixture` that inject dependencies, setup data, or configure state for test functions.
questions.source_text: What is a 'fixture' in `pytest`?

questions.title: How do you request a fixture within a test function?
options: A. By calling the fixture function inside the test body
C. By including the fixture name as an argument in the test function signature
D. By importing it from a global config file
questions.explanation: Pytest uses dependency injection; if a test function argument matches a fixture name, pytest automatically runs the fixture and passes the result.
questions.source_text: How do you request a fixture within a test function?

questions.title: Which file is used to share fixtures across multiple test files in a directory without importing them?
questions.explanation: `conftest.py` is a special file recognized by pytest to provide local plugins and shared fixtures for an entire directory.
questions.source_text: Which file is used to share fixtures across multiple test files in a directory without importing them?

questions.title: How can you run tests that are marked with a specific label, such as `@pytest.mark.slow`?
questions.explanation: The `-m` flag stands for 'mark' and allows you to filter and run tests based on custom markers.
questions.source_text: How can you run tests that are marked with a specific label, such as `@pytest.mark.slow`?

questions.title: Which decorator is used to run the same test function multiple times with different input values?
questions.explanation: `@pytest.mark.parametrize` allows you to define a set of arguments for a test, creating a separate test case for each set of data.
questions.source_text: Which decorator is used to run the same test function multiple times with different input values?

questions.title: How do you check that a specific block of code raises an expected exception in `pytest`?
questions.explanation: `pytest.raises` is used as a context manager to intercept and verify exceptions raised by the enclosed code.
questions.source_text: How do you check that a specific block of code raises an expected exception in `pytest`?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the `yield` keyword inside a `pytest` fixture?
options: A. To make the fixture a generator for multiple values
B. To provide a value to the test and then execute teardown code afterward
C. To pause the test execution until a manual trigger
D. To return a list of all tests using that fixture
questions.explanation: In a 'yield fixture', the code before `yield` is the setup, the yielded value is the fixture data, and the code after `yield` is the teardown.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of the `yield` keyword inside a `pytest` fixture?

questions.title: What does the `-x` flag do when running pytest?
options: A. Runs only the tests that failed in the last run
B. Stops the test execution immediately after the first failure
C. Excludes all tests marked as 'experimental'
D. Deletes all cache files before running
questions.explanation: The `-x` (or `--exitfirst`) flag is useful for debugging when you want to stop as soon as any test fails.
questions.source_text: What does the `-x` flag do when running pytest?

questions.title: Which command-line argument allows you to see the values of local variables in the traceback of a failed test?
questions.explanation: The `--showlocals` flag is extremely helpful for debugging as it prints the state of all local variables at the point of failure.
questions.source_text: Which command-line argument allows you to see the values of local variables in the traceback of a failed test?

questions.title: What is the 'scope' of a fixture if it is set to `scope='module'`?
options: A. The fixture is created once per test function
B. The fixture is created once per test file (module)
C. The fixture is created once per directory
D. The fixture is created once per test session
questions.explanation: Fixtures can be scoped to 'function' (default), 'class', 'module', 'package', or 'session' to control how often the setup/teardown logic runs.
questions.source_text: What is the 'scope' of a fixture if it is set to `scope='module'`?

questions.title: What is the difference between `@pytest.mark.skip` and `@pytest.mark.xfail`?
options: B. skip bypasses the test; xfail runs it but expects it to fail
C. skip is for bugs; xfail is for features
D. xfail is only for Windows systems
questions.explanation: `skip` completely ignores the test, while `xfail` (expected failure) still executes the test; if the test unexpectedly passes, it is reported as XPASS.
questions.source_text: What is the difference between `@pytest.mark.skip` and `@pytest.mark.xfail`?

questions.title: Which base class must you inherit from to create a new test case in the `unittest` framework?
questions.explanation: The `unittest.TestCase` class provide the infrastructure for creating individual tests and provides various assert methods to check for failures.
questions.source_text: Which base class must you inherit from to create a new test case in the `unittest` framework?

questions.title: What is the naming convention for methods that `unittest` automatically identifies as test cases?
options: D. They must include 'check' in the name
questions.explanation: By default, the `unittest` test loader only picks up methods whose names start with the string 'test'.
questions.source_text: What is the naming convention for methods that `unittest` automatically identifies as test cases?

questions.title: Which method is called immediately BEFORE each individual test method is executed?
questions.explanation: `setUp()` is a special method used to prepare the 'test fixture' (like creating database connections or initializing objects) before every test run.
questions.source_text: Which method is called immediately BEFORE each individual test method is executed?

questions.title: Which method is called immediately AFTER each individual test method is executed, regardless of whether the test passed or failed?
questions.explanation: `tearDown()` is used to clean up resources after each test to ensure a clean state for the next test case.
questions.source_text: Which method is called immediately AFTER each individual test method is executed, regardless of whether the test passed or failed?

questions.title: Which assertion method would you use to verify that a function call raises a specific exception?
questions.explanation: `assertRaises()` is used as a context manager (or a direct call) to ensure that the code block inside it triggers the expected exception type.
questions.source_text: Which assertion method would you use to verify that a function call raises a specific exception?

questions.title: How can you run all tests in a module from the command line using the `unittest` command-line interface?
questions.explanation: Using the `-m` flag to run the `unittest` module followed by the module name is the standard CLI execution method.
questions.source_text: How can you run all tests in a module from the command line using the `unittest` command-line interface?

questions.title: What does an 'E' (Error) signify in the `unittest` output, as opposed to an 'F' (Failure)?
options: A. The test took too long to run
C. An unexpected exception occurred outside of an assertion
D. The test file was not found
questions.explanation: A Failure ('F') means an assertion didn't match. An Error ('E') means the code crashed or raised an exception that wasn't being explicitly tested.
questions.source_text: What does an 'E' (Error) signify in the `unittest` output, as opposed to an 'F' (Failure)?

questions.title: Which decorator is used to skip a test method if a specific condition is not met?
questions.explanation: The `@unittest.skipIf(condition, reason)` decorator allows you to bypass tests based on environmental factors like OS type or Python version.
questions.source_text: Which decorator is used to skip a test method if a specific condition is not met?

questions.title: What is a 'Test Suite' in the `unittest` framework?
options: A. A collection of test cases or other test suites
B. A document containing the test results
C. A high-level class that runs all tests in the project
D. A special folder for test files
questions.explanation: A `TestSuite` object is used to aggregate individual tests that should be run together, providing a way to organize complex testing cycles.
questions.source_text: What is a 'Test Suite' in the `unittest` framework?

questions.title: Which method should you use to compare two floating-point numbers for equality within a certain margin of error?
questions.explanation: `assertAlmostEqual()` allows for floating-point imprecision by checking if the difference between two values is within a specific number of decimal places.
questions.source_text: Which method should you use to compare two floating-point numbers for equality within a certain margin of error?

questions.title: Which class in the `unittest.mock` module is the most commonly used to replace parts of your system under test?
questions.explanation: `Mock` is the flexible base class used to create objects that can be used in place of real objects to record how they are used.
questions.source_text: Which class in the `unittest.mock` module is the most commonly used to replace parts of your system under test?

questions.title: What is the primary difference between `Mock` and `MagicMock`?
options: A. MagicMock can only be used with Python 2
B. MagicMock implements common magic (dunder) methods by default
C. Mock is asynchronous, MagicMock is synchronous
D. MagicMock is faster but consumes more memory
questions.explanation: `MagicMock` is a subclass of `Mock` that has default implementations of most Python 'magic' methods (like `__getitem__`, `__iter__`, etc.) already available.
questions.source_text: What is the primary difference between `Mock` and `MagicMock`?

questions.title: Which decorator/context manager is used to temporarily replace an object at a specific string path with a mock?
questions.explanation: `patch` handles the lookup and replacement of an object during a test, automatically restoring the original object once the test completes.
questions.source_text: Which decorator/context manager is used to temporarily replace an object at a specific string path with a mock?

questions.title: When using `patch('package.module.ClassName')`, which object should you target for patching?
options: A. Where the object is defined
B. Where the object is looked up/imported
C. Always the root level of the package
questions.explanation: You should patch where the object is *used* (looked up). If `module_a` imports `ClassName` from `module_b`, you should patch `module_a.ClassName`.
questions.source_text: When using `patch('package.module.ClassName')`, which object should you target for patching?

questions.title: How do you make a mock object return a specific value when called?
questions.explanation: The `return_value` attribute defines the result returned when the mock object is invoked as a function.
questions.source_text: How do you make a mock object return a specific value when called?

questions.title: What attribute allows a mock to return different values on consecutive calls or raise an exception?
questions.explanation: `side_effect` can take a list (returning values in order), a function (returning the function's result), or an exception class/instance to be raised.
questions.source_text: What attribute allows a mock to return different values on consecutive calls or raise an exception?

questions.title: Which method is used to verify that a mock was called at least once with specific arguments?
questions.explanation: `assert_called_with()` verifies that the last call made to the mock was with the specified arguments.
questions.source_text: Which method is used to verify that a mock was called at least once with specific arguments?

questions.title: What is the purpose of the `spec` argument when creating a mock?
options: A. To speed up the mock execution
B. To limit the mock to only the attributes and methods present on a specific object
C. To define the return type of the mock
D. To provide a documentation string for the mock
questions.explanation: Specifying a `spec` prevents the mock from allowing access to arbitrary attributes that don't exist on the original class, helping catch typos in test code.
questions.source_text: What is the purpose of the `spec` argument when creating a mock?

questions.title: Which `patch` variant is used to replace dictionary values within a test?
questions.explanation: `patch.dict` is specifically designed to patch dictionary-like objects, such as `os.environ`.
questions.source_text: Which `patch` variant is used to replace dictionary values within a test?

questions.title: How can you access a list of all calls made to a mock object?
questions.explanation: `call_args_list` is a list of `call` objects representing every time the mock was invoked, including the arguments used.
questions.source_text: How can you access a list of all calls made to a mock object?

questions.title: In `unittest.mock`, what does `PropertyMock` do?
options: A. Mocks a class attribute that is protected
B. Mocks a value that is treated as a property rather than a method
C. Ensures a mock cannot be modified
D. Mocks the metadata of a module
questions.explanation: `PropertyMock` is used when you need to mock an attribute that is defined as a `@property` on a class.
questions.source_text: In `unittest.mock`, what does `PropertyMock` do?

questions.title: What is 'autospeccing' in the context of `patch`?
options: A. Automatically generating documentation for mocks
B. Creating a mock that automatically has the same attributes and signature as the object it replaces
C. Automatically mocking every module in a package
D. Validating that a mock returns the correct data type
questions.explanation: Passing `autospec=True` to `patch` creates a mock that behaves like the object it replaces, including enforcing function signatures so calls with wrong arguments fail.
questions.source_text: What is 'autospeccing' in the context of `patch`?

questions.title: Which function creates intermediate directories if they don’t exist?
questions.explanation: os.makedirs(path) creates all intermediate-level directories needed to contain the leaf directory.
questions.source_text: Which function creates intermediate directories if they don’t exist?

questions.title: Which function removes a file?
questions.explanation: os.remove(path) deletes the specified file.
questions.source_text: Which function removes a file?

questions.title: Which function removes an empty directory?
questions.explanation: os.rmdir(path) removes an empty directory.
questions.source_text: Which function removes an empty directory?

questions.title: Which function lists all files and directories in a given path?
questions.explanation: os.listdir(path) returns a list of entries in the given directory.
questions.source_text: Which function lists all files and directories in a given path?

questions.title: Which function returns the absolute path of a file?
questions.explanation: os.path.abspath(path) returns the absolute path of the given file or directory.
questions.source_text: Which function returns the absolute path of a file?

questions.title: Which function splits a path into directory and file components?
questions.explanation: os.path.split(path) returns a tuple (head, tail) where head is the directory and tail is the file name.
questions.source_text: Which function splits a path into directory and file components?

questions.title: Which function retrieves the value of an environment variable?
questions.explanation: os.getenv('VAR_NAME') returns the value of the specified environment variable or None if not set.
questions.source_text: Which function retrieves the value of an environment variable?

questions.title: Which attribute provides direct access to all environment variables as a dictionary?
questions.explanation: os.environ is a dictionary-like object containing the current environment variables.
questions.source_text: Which attribute provides direct access to all environment variables as a dictionary?

questions.title: Which method sets a new environment variable in Python?
questions.explanation: Assigning to os.environ['VAR'] sets or updates an environment variable.

questions.title: Which function removes an environment variable?
questions.explanation: Deleting the key from os.environ removes the environment variable.

questions.title: Which environment variable typically stores the system PATH?
questions.explanation: PATH contains directories searched for executable programs.
